items.explanation: The passage argues the self is a moving judgement revised whenever the reference group changes, with examples of salary and body image shifting after comparison. options: Because people judge themselves mainly by comparing themselves with others, so the judgement changes when the reference group changes

Because self-esteem rises and falls only with income and social status
Because psychologists have proved that private feelings do not exist at all
items.passage: Self-esteem is usually described as a private possession, something a person either has or lacks, like height or a bank balance. Yet the evidence of everyday life points in a different direction. People rarely assess themselves in isolation. They assess themselves against neighbours, colleagues, classmates and strangers on screens, and the verdict shifts with every new comparison. A salary that felt generous becomes inadequate the moment a peer earns more. A body that felt comfortable becomes a source of shame after an hour spent looking at curated photographs. The self, in this account, is not a fixed object to be measured but a moving judgement, revised whenever the reference group changes. This does not mean self-esteem is unreal. It means it is relational, and therefore fragile in a world where comparisons multiply. Social media did not invent comparison, but it industrialised it. Earlier generations compared themselves with a few dozen people they knew. A modern user compares herself with thousands, many of them selected precisely because they excel at the very thing she doubts in herself. The comparison is also asymmetric. We see other people's highlights and our own unedited footage, so we conclude that everyone else is coping better. Psychologists call this the spotlight of selective attention, and it explains why even successful people report feeling behind. The remedy often proposed is to stop comparing, but that advice misunderstands the mechanism. Comparison is not a habit we can simply drop; it is how the mind locates itself. A more useful remedy is to choose the comparison deliberately. Compare present performance with past performance, rather than with a stranger's best moment. Ask whether the standard is one you endorse or one that was imposed on you. And notice that the people we envy are themselves comparing upward, trapped in the same chain. None of this makes insecurity vanish. It does, however, change its character. Insecurity that is recognised as relational can be questioned, while insecurity treated as a personal defect can only be endured. The difference matters because it decides whether a person seeks a better mirror or a better life. The same logic operates in workplaces and schools, where ranking systems make comparison unavoidable and often public. A student who scores well may still feel inadequate beside a classmate who scores better, and an employee praised by a manager may still feel overlooked when a colleague is promoted first. Institutions that publish league tables and leaderboards assume that comparison motivates, yet the evidence suggests it often demoralises those in the middle, who compare upward and conclude they are failing. A wiser design would compare people with their own earlier performance, and would celebrate progress that is invisible in a ranking. That shift does not remove ambition, but it changes its direction, from beating others to becoming better than one was, which is a contest a person can actually win.

items.explanation: The passage states a metaphor selects some features and hides others and thereby shapes what we think can be done, with examples of argument as battle and time as money. It explicitly says thought without metaphor is impossible, so elimination and mere decoration are rejected, and it stresses that different backgrounds use different metaphors.
options: Metaphors are decorative language with no effect on how people think or act
Metaphors are useful only in poetry and should be avoided in serious discussion
Metaphors organise thought by selecting some features and hiding others, shaping what actions seem possible
Metaphors always mislead, so clear thinking requires eliminating them entirely
Metaphors are identical across cultures, which is why translation is easy
items.passage: We speak of arguments as battles, of time as money, of ideas as food to be digested. Such metaphors are so familiar that we forget they are metaphors at all, and we begin to treat them as descriptions of how the world is. Yet a metaphor is not a neutral label. It selects some features of a thing and hides others, and in doing so it shapes what we think can be done about it. If an argument is a battle, then winning matters more than understanding, and conceding a point feels like defeat. If time is money, then an unhurried afternoon feels like a waste, and rest needs a justification in the language of investment. The metaphor does not merely decorate thought; it organises it. This matters most when people from different backgrounds try to understand each other. Two speakers may use the same words while living inside different metaphors, so they talk past each other without knowing why. A manager who thinks of a team as a machine will look for broken parts when performance falls, while a colleague who thinks of a team as a garden will look for soil, light and patience. Neither picture is wrong in itself, but each makes certain remedies visible and others invisible. Mutual understanding, then, is not only a matter of clearer definitions. It requires noticing the metaphors each side is using and asking what those metaphors allow and forbid. Sometimes the task is to translate, finding a shared metaphor both can inhabit. Sometimes it is to hold two metaphors at once, accepting that a marriage can be both a partnership and a journey, or that a market can be both a competition and a conversation. The danger is not metaphor itself, since thought without metaphor is impossible, but the unexamined metaphor, the one that has hardened into common sense. When we mistake our favourite metaphor for the thing itself, we lose the freedom to think differently, and with it the chance to understand someone whose metaphor is not our own. The same problem appears in diplomacy and in business, where negotiators from different cultures use the same words while meaning different things. One side may speak of partnership and mean equality, while the other speaks of partnership and means hierarchy, and each leaves the meeting believing an agreement has been reached. Only later, when expectations collide, does the misunderstanding surface, by which time blame is easier than translation. Skilled negotiators therefore spend as much time on the metaphors in the room as on the numbers on the table, asking what each side assumes about trust, about time and about obligation. That attention is slow and unglamorous, but it is the difference between an agreement that holds and one that collapses at the first test.

items.passage: Liberal democracy is often defended as the rule of the majority, yet its most distinctive feature is the protection it offers to those who lose. Elections decide who governs, but constitutions, courts, a free press and the right to dissent decide whether losing remains bearable. Without those protections, majority rule can become a polite name for the domination of a minority, and the loser has no reason to accept the result except fear. This is why dissent is not a luxury that democracy tolerates when times are easy. It is the mechanism by which democracy corrects itself. A society that punishes criticism may enjoy quiet for a while, but it loses the information it needs to recognise its own mistakes. Policies go unchallenged, errors compound, and by the time the failure becomes undeniable, the institutions that might have corrected it have already been weakened. Critics of dissent argue that constant criticism paralyses government and erodes trust. There is force in the worry. A democracy in which every decision is treated as illegitimate cannot act. But the remedy is not silence; it is the discipline of dissent, criticism that is specific, evidence based and open to reply. Such dissent strengthens trust rather than eroding it, because citizens can see that power is being watched and that mistakes can be named without punishment. The deeper threat, therefore, is not noisy disagreement but the quiet consensus that forms when people learn it is safer not to speak. A democracy can survive losing an election, losing a debate, even losing a generation's confidence. What it cannot survive is the loss of the habit of dissent itself, for once that habit is gone, elections continue but they no longer decide anything that matters, because no one dares to propose an alternative. The media plays a part in this, because outrage is easier to report than deliberation, and a democracy that is always shouting can mistake volume for vitality. A quiet citizen who reads carefully, votes thoughtfully and discusses politics with neighbours may contribute more to democratic health than a loud commentator who treats every disagreement as treason. Yet the quiet citizen is invisible in the news, while the loud commentator is everywhere, and young people learning what citizenship looks like may conclude that democracy is a contest of insults. Restoring the habit of dissent therefore requires restoring the habit of listening, and that is a cultural task as much as a constitutional one, learned in schools, in families and in workplaces long before it is tested in parliament.

options: Trolling is ordinary behaviour made easier by anonymity, distance and platform rewards for outrage

Trolling is a new form of behaviour with no connection to ordinary social life

items.passage: The internet troll is often portrayed as a monster, a person of unusual cruelty who seeks out victims for pleasure. That portrait is comforting because it places the problem outside ordinary life. The less comforting truth is that trolling is often ordinary behaviour made easier by design. Anonymity removes the social costs that normally restrain hostility: no one sees the speaker blush, no neighbour will mention the remark tomorrow, no reputation is at stake. Distance does the rest. The target is a username, not a face, so empathy, which depends heavily on visible cues, has little to work with. The platform adds its own incentives. Outrage travels faster than nuance, so the comment that provokes a reaction is rewarded with attention, while the careful reply sinks unseen. None of this excuses the troll, but it changes the diagnosis. If trolling were only the work of a few disturbed individuals, removing them would solve it. If it is a predictable response to anonymity, distance and reward, then removing individuals merely creates vacancies that the same conditions will fill. The remedy, then, is not only moral condemnation but redesign. Real names are one proposal, but they carry their own costs, silencing dissidents and vulnerable people who need anonymity to speak safely. A better approach may be to change the rewards: slow down replies, make the human being behind a post more visible, and deny attention to provocation rather than amplifying it. What is at stake is not politeness alone. A public square in which the loudest and cruelest voices dominate is one in which quieter people withdraw, and the conversation that remains is not a debate but a performance of cruelty for an audience that has learned to watch rather than participate. Designers of platforms face a choice that is rarely described as a moral one, yet it shapes public life more than many laws. A reply button that rewards speed will produce heat, while a design that asks a user to pause before posting may produce reflection. A feed that shows the most provocative comment first will teach users that provocation is the way to be seen, while a feed that shows the most thoughtful reply first will teach a different lesson. None of these choices is neutral, and none can be avoided by claiming that a platform merely reflects its users. Platforms do not only reflect behaviour; they train it, day after day, in millions of small interactions, and the public square they create is the sum of those design decisions, not an accident of human nature.

items.explanation: The passage says humans fear the rare catastrophe more than familiar harm even when the latter kills more, and that probabilities answer a different question from trust, blame and truth telling. Fuel scarcity, uncalculated probabilities and higher total deaths from nuclear accidents are all contradicted by the passage.
options: Because the public does not understand that nuclear power produces no carbon dioxide
Because nuclear fuel is too scarce to power a city for months
Because people weigh dreaded, vivid, sudden catastrophes more heavily than familiar slow harms, and because the real question is about trust in institutions
Because engineers have never calculated the probability of an accident
Because nuclear accidents kill more people in total than coal pollution
items.passage: Nuclear fission presents a paradox that no amount of engineering can fully resolve. On paper it is among the cleanest ways to generate large amounts of electricity, producing almost no carbon dioxide while running, and its fuel is astonishingly dense: a small quantity can power a city for months. Yet public fear of nuclear power remains intense, and that fear is not simply ignorance. It reflects a judgement about the kind of risk involved. A coal plant harms many people slowly, through air pollution spread over decades, while a nuclear accident harms few people suddenly, in a way that is vivid, memorable and dreaded. Human beings weigh dread heavily. They fear the rare catastrophe more than the familiar harm, even when the familiar harm kills far more people in total. Engineers respond by pointing to probabilities, and the probabilities are indeed low. But probabilities answer a different question from the one the public is asking. The public is not asking how likely an accident is; it is asking who will be blamed, who will be protected, and whether the institutions in charge can be trusted to tell the truth when something goes wrong. Trust, once lost, is not restored by a better statistic. It is restored by institutions that admit uncertainty, share information promptly, and accept independent scrutiny even when it is inconvenient. The future of nuclear power, therefore, depends less on the next reactor design than on the next institutional failure. A technology can be safe in the laboratory sense and still be rejected if the organisations around it are not believed. Conversely, a society that trusts its regulators may accept risks that look frightening on paper. The lesson extends beyond energy. Whenever a risk is dreaded rather than merely frequent, technical reassurance alone will fail, because the argument is not about numbers but about whether the people who manage the risk deserve to be believed. The same pattern appears with other dreaded risks, from vaccines to genetically modified food, where a rare, vivid harm looms larger in the mind than a common, invisible one. A parent may fear a rare side effect more than the disease it prevents, not because the numbers support that fear but because the side effect is vivid and the disease is abstract. Experts who respond with statistics alone miss the point, because the fear is not about probability but about control, about whether a parent feels she is choosing a risk or having it imposed on her. Communication that acknowledges that feeling, that explains who bears the risk and who benefits, and that admits what is still unknown, is more persuasive than a chart, because it treats the public as a partner in judgement rather than as a pupil to be corrected.

items.passage: The telegram came at dusk, in a yellow envelope, / and my grandmother read it twice before she spoke. / Four lines, no more, for a life that had crossed oceans. // She folded the paper as if it were a letter, / and placed it in the tin where she kept her keys, / beside the ration card and the photograph of my grandfather. // That night she cooked as usual, salt in the dal, / cumin in the pan, the radio low beside the stove, / and when I asked if she was sad, she said, / Sad is a word for people who have time to sit. // Years later I found the telegram, the ink now faded, / the yellow turned the colour of weak tea, / and I understood what she had not said: / that grief, when it has nowhere to go, learns to cook, / to fold, to keep the keys, to carry on.

items.passage: Sunrise Foods is a regional biscuit maker with a 40-year history in western India. Its flagship glucose biscuit once held 18 percent of the regional market, but over the last 18 months its share has fallen to 12 percent. A new rival sells a similar biscuit at 20 percent below Sunrise prices, using cheaper palm oil, thinner packaging and a direct-to-shop distribution model that skips wholesalers. Sunrise buys better wheat and butter, pays its 300 factory workers above the local average, and sells through a network of 400 distributors who have stocked its products for decades. The marketing head wants to match the rival price by switching to cheaper ingredients and cutting distributor margins, arguing that market share is the only measure that matters and that quality differences are invisible to most buyers. The operations head warns that cheaper ingredients would break the taste that loyal customers recognise, while the sales head warns that cutting distributor margins would push distributors to promote the rival instead. The finance head has calculated that matching the price would need a 15 percent cost cut, which cannot be achieved without changing both the recipe and the distribution terms. Meanwhile, a survey of 2,000 buyers shows that 60 percent buy mainly on price, 25 percent buy mainly on taste and trust, and 15 percent buy whichever brand their local shop recommends. The founder, who still chairs the board, is torn between protecting the brand built over four decades and accepting that the market has changed. A decision is needed before the festive season, when biscuit sales double and shelf space is fixed for three months.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support the decision to match the rival price by cutting costs?

items.explanation: A separate lower-priced pack under a different name protects the flagship recipe and distributor relationships while giving price-sensitive buyers an option, so it serves both segments without destroying the brand. Cutting the price and changing the recipe at once destroys the taste advantage. Advertising alone does not change the price gap. Asking distributors to absorb the cut would push them to promote the rival.
options: Cut the price immediately across all packs and change the recipe in the same week
Launch a separate lower-priced pack with a different brand name while keeping the flagship recipe and price unchanged
Keep the current price and spend the festive budget on advertising the existing product
Ask distributors to absorb the entire price cut without any change to their contracts
Raise the price by 10 percent to signal premium quality
items.question: What should Sunrise Foods do before the festive season?

items.explanation: If the taste-driven minority delivers nearly half the revenue, losing them by changing the recipe would cost far more than the price-sensitive buyers gained, which directly undermines the share-first argument. The rival gaining shelf space strengthens rather than weakens the case for action. The festive share and palm oil prices do not address the revenue concentration. Distributor demands are a separate negotiation issue.
options: The rival has just signed a contract with a large retail chain that will double its shelf space
The festive season accounts for only a small share of annual biscuit sales
The 25 percent of buyers who buy on taste and trust account for 45 percent of Sunrise revenue because they buy larger packs more often
Palm oil prices have fallen sharply in the last three months
Several distributors have asked Sunrise for higher margins this year
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the marketing head's argument for matching the rival price?

items.explanation: Prior crash-test passes for a nearly identical vehicle would remove the core safety objection, which is the only serious argument against the fast option. A clean delivery record and dealer pressure do not make an untested part safe. Rivals facing the same shortage does not change the safety question. A discount is irrelevant to whether the part is safe to fit.
options: The maker has never missed a delivery deadline before
Dealers have asked the maker to keep production running at any cost
The rival firms are also facing the same supplier fire
The overseas casing has already passed the same crash tests for a nearly identical vehicle sold in another country
The overseas supplier has offered a 10 percent discount on the first order
items.passage: A mid-sized maker of electric two-wheelers depends on a single supplier in another state for a specialised battery casing. A fire at the supplier plant has halted production for at least six weeks, and the maker has only three weeks of casing stock. No other supplier in the country makes the exact casing, and retooling a new supplier would take ten weeks and cost a large sum. The maker has 8,000 confirmed customer orders with delivery promises, and its dealers have already collected advances. The purchase head has found an overseas supplier that can deliver a slightly different casing in two weeks, but it has not been crash-tested with this vehicle, and the engineering head warns that fitting it without full testing could create a safety risk. The sales head wants to accept the overseas casing immediately and tell customers nothing about the change, arguing that any delay will push buyers to rivals and that the casing difference is minor. The legal head warns that an untested change to a safety-related part could expose the firm to liability and a recall. The chief executive must decide this week, because the overseas supplier needs a firm order and a 50 percent advance. A second option is to pause production, inform customers of a six-week delay, and offer refunds or a free accessory as compensation, which would protect safety but lose an estimated 30 percent of orders to rivals. The firm also has 200 dealers who have paid for showroom branding and who will lose festival-season sales if production stops. The engineering team says a partial test of the overseas casing could be done in ten days, but a full crash test would take six weeks. The overseas supplier has asked for a non-refundable advance, and the firm's bank has warned that the advance would breach a loan condition if production is later halted.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support accepting the overseas casing immediately?

items.explanation: If buyers rank safety above speed, a transparent delay protects the trust that drives future sales, while a rushed untested part risks the very attribute buyers value most. The supplier being late is a secondary concern. Cash for refunds makes a delay affordable but does not show it is the better choice. The cause of the fire and the executive promise do not weigh on customer priorities.
options: The overseas supplier has a reputation for delivering late
The maker has enough cash to pay refunds to all customers who cancel
The supplier plant fire was caused by an electrical fault that could recur
The chief executive has personally promised dealers that production will not stop
A recent survey shows that most buyers of this vehicle rank safety above delivery speed when choosing a brand
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support pausing production and informing customers of the delay?

items.explanation: The higher unit cost is a commercial drawback, not a reason to reject the secrecy itself, and a more expensive part could still be acceptable if it were tested and disclosed. The other four options all directly attack the proposal: liability, loss of trust, regulatory disclosure duties, and denying customers an informed choice.
options: The overseas casing costs more per unit than the original casing
An untested safety-related change creates liability and recall risk
Customers who learn later that a part was changed without disclosure will lose trust in the brand
Regulators require disclosure of material changes to safety-related components
Silence removes the chance for customers to make an informed choice about waiting
items.question: All of the following are valid reasons to reject the sales head's proposal to fit the overseas casing without telling customers EXCEPT

items.explanation: If most users would delete the app on learning of the sale, the deal destroys the user base it depends on and is commercially self-defeating as well as a breach of trust. Payment in instalments does not change the consent problem. A possible price rise is a separate alternative, not evidence against the sale. The buyer having a good research record does not cure the lack of informed consent. A past unnoticed sharing does not prove users consented.
options: The data buyer has offered to pay in instalments over two years
A recent study showed that 85 percent of users would delete the app if they learned their health data had been sold
The premium subscription price could be raised by a small amount without losing many subscribers
The analytics firm has published respected public-health research in the past
The company has already shared anonymised data once before without any complaint
items.passage: A health-tracking app with two million users in India records sleep, steps, heart rate and self-reported mood. The app is free, and its revenue comes from premium subscriptions taken by only 4 percent of users. The company is running out of cash and has been offered a large payment by a data analytics firm for access to anonymised user data, which the buyer says it will use only for public-health research. The privacy policy, written in dense legal language, says data may be shared with partners for research purposes, but the sign-up screen never explained this clearly and most users believe their health data stays private. The product head argues that anonymised data cannot identify anyone, so no user is harmed, and that the sale is the only way to keep the app free and avoid layoffs. The data protection officer warns that health data, even without names, can often be re-identified by combining it with other datasets, and that users never gave informed consent. The legal adviser notes that the law in this area is still evolving and that a regulator could later rule the sale unlawful. The founders must decide before the next funding round, because the data buyer wants an exclusive deal signed within two weeks and the company payroll for the next quarter depends on the payment. The app has 40,000 paying subscribers and a rating of 4.2 stars, and its reviews often mention privacy as a reason for trust. The data buyer is a large analytics firm that has previously bought health data from other apps and published research based on it. The company's investors have asked for a plan to reach profitability within a year, and the founders have told staff that no layoffs are planned if the data deal is signed. The app's terms of service were last updated two years ago.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support refusing the data sale?
items.set_title: DM3: The Health App Data Sale

items.explanation: Seeking clear, specific consent with an honest explanation of purpose and risk respects user autonomy and creates a lawful basis for sharing, while limiting the sale to consenting users. Selling first and informing later, selling dormant users data, or giving it away free all bypass consent. Closing the app is a disproportionate response when a consent-based path exists.
options: Sell the data now and inform users afterwards in a brief email
Sell only the data of users who have not opened the app in six months
Ask users for clear, specific consent to share anonymised data for research, explaining the purpose and the re-identification risk, and proceed only with data from users who agree
Share the data for free so that the transaction cannot be called a sale
Stop collecting health data entirely and close the app
items.question: What is the most defensible course of action for the company?
items.set_title: DM3: The Health App Data Sale

items.explanation: Demonstrated re-identification from as few as four data points directly contradicts the claim that removing names makes users safe, since the dataset holds far more than four points per user. Collecting more data than rivals or storing it abroad does not by itself prove re-identification is possible. Usage time is irrelevant. Never having been fined says nothing about whether harm is possible.
options: The app collects more data points than its competitors do
Users spend an average of 20 minutes a day on the app
The analytics firm stores data on servers in another country
Researchers have re-identified individuals in similar health datasets using only four data points
The company has never been fined by a regulator
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the product head's claim that anonymised data cannot harm any user?
items.set_title: DM3: The Health App Data Sale

items.explanation: Extra tender marks for open competition turn the appointment into a direct commercial advantage for the firm, strengthening the case for the deputy beyond fairness alone. A lower salary from the nephew does not offset inexperience in a role of this scale. A family promise and the deputy staying do not support choosing the deputy. The branch manager withdrawing removes one alternative but does not favour the deputy over the nephew.
options: The nephew has offered to take a lower salary than the deputy
The founder has promised the nephew the role in front of the extended family
The deputy has said he will stay even if the nephew is appointed
The branch manager has withdrawn her application for personal reasons
The government tender awards extra marks for firms whose senior roles are filled through open competition
items.passage: A family-owned logistics firm with 800 employees is run by a founder who is preparing to retire. The founder wants the vacant post of regional head, a role that controls a budget of 40 crore rupees and a team of 120 people, to go to a nephew who joined the firm two years ago after a management degree abroad. The nephew is bright and hardworking but has managed only a team of six and has no experience of union negotiations, which the regional role requires every year. Two internal candidates have applied: a deputy with 14 years in the firm who has run large teams and handled three union settlements, and a branch manager with 11 years who has doubled the revenue of her branch. The human resources head has warned the founder privately that appointing the nephew will be seen as nepotism, will damage morale, and could trigger the resignation of the deputy, who has already been approached by a rival. The founder argues that family ownership gives the family the right to choose, that the nephew can learn on the job with mentoring, and that the deputy can be retained with a higher salary. The board, which includes two independent directors, must approve the appointment. The firm is also in the middle of a tender for a large government contract, and the tender documents require disclosure of any senior appointment made through a family relationship. The two independent directors have asked for the selection criteria in writing before the board meeting, and the tender authority has set a deadline of three weeks for the disclosure. The deputy has been with the firm since it had only 50 employees and is known to the largest clients by name. The branch manager has said she will accept the board's decision either way, but the deputy has not given any such assurance.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support appointing the deputy instead of the nephew?

items.explanation: A record of two recent on-the-job failures in this exact role shows that learning while doing is a proven risk here, not a safe assumption. A short negotiation course does not outweigh that record. Willing mentors, a manual and the founder staying as adviser would support, not weaken, the learning argument.
options: The last two people who learned this role on the job both failed within a year and cost the firm major clients
The nephew has completed a short course on negotiation
The deputy is willing to mentor the nephew for six months
The regional role has a detailed operations manual
The founder is willing to stay on as an adviser for one year
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the founder's argument that the nephew can learn on the job with mentoring?

items.explanation: An open criteria-based process with disclosure gives the nephew a fair chance while protecting the firm from charges of nepotism and from tender non-compliance. Immediate approval ignores merit and morale risks. A blanket family ban is disproportionate. Indefinite delay leaves a critical role vacant. Secrecy compounds the problem once it emerges.
options: Approve the nephew immediately to respect the founder's wishes
Run an open, criteria-based selection for the role, assess all three candidates against the same standards, and disclose any family relationship in the tender as required
Reject the nephew outright and bar family members from all future senior roles
Delay the appointment indefinitely until the tender is decided
Appoint the nephew but keep the decision secret from employees
items.question: What should the board do?

items.explanation: If the largest client stays regardless, the main cost of disciplining the representative disappears, so the promotion can be judged on conduct rather than fear of losing revenue. High product knowledge and a raised target argue for keeping the person productive, not for promoting. A private apology to one colleague does not undo a pattern. Never having denied a promotion before is precedent, not a reason.
options: The representative has the highest product knowledge scores in the team
The team revenue target for next year has been raised by 20 percent
The representative's largest client has said it will stay with the company even if the representative leaves
The representative has apologised privately to one junior colleague
The company has never denied a promotion to a top seller before
items.passage: A pharmaceutical sales team of 18 people has one representative who brings in 35 percent of the team's revenue, far more than anyone else. The same representative routinely misses reporting deadlines, takes credit for colleagues' client introductions, and has made two junior colleagues cry in team meetings with public criticism. Three team members have asked the regional manager for transfers in the last two months, and the human resources team has received an informal complaint about bullying. The representative's clients are loyal to the individual rather than the company, and the manager fears that disciplining the person could cost the team its largest accounts. The manager's own bonus depends partly on team revenue, which creates a conflict of interest. The company has a written code of conduct that requires respectful behaviour and accurate credit for work, and it applies to all employees regardless of performance. The regional manager must decide before the annual appraisal cycle, when the representative expects the highest rating and a promotion to senior representative, a move that would give the person authority over the very colleagues who complained. The human resources team has a written record of the informal complaint and of the two transfer requests, and it has advised the manager that the code of conduct requires a formal investigation once a bullying complaint is received. The representative's clients include the team's three largest accounts, and two of those clients have said they value the representative's speed in answering calls. The annual appraisal cycle ends in four weeks, and the promotion decision must be recorded with reasons that the human resources team can defend if it is challenged later.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support denying the promotion?

items.explanation: If clients buy for product quality and the service network, the accounts are tied to the company rather than the individual, so discipline is far less costly than feared. Juniors leaving and the representative threatening to resign would strengthen the fear. The bonus link explains the manager's bias but does not change the client facts. Rival interest in the representative is a risk, not evidence about client loyalty.
options: Two junior colleagues have already found jobs with a rival firm
The representative has threatened to resign if disciplined
The manager's bonus is linked to team revenue
The clients buy mainly because of the company's product quality and service network, not because of any single representative
The rival firms have been trying to recruit the representative for a year
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the manager's fear that discipline will cost the largest accounts?

items.explanation: Being the highest earner is a reason the manager might hesitate, not a reason to act; it argues for caution rather than intervention. The code applying to everyone, the transfer requests, the promotion risk, and the signal sent by inaction are all genuine reasons to act now.
options: The code of conduct applies to all employees regardless of performance
Three transfer requests and a bullying complaint show the behaviour is already damaging the team
Promoting the person would put the representative in authority over the complainants
Ignoring the conduct signals to the team that revenue excuses bullying
The representative is the highest earner on the team
items.question: All of the following are valid reasons to act against the representative's behaviour now EXCEPT

items.explanation: Broad employee preference for a temporary cut over job losses makes the pay cut the option most likely to be accepted and to avoid a strike, which is the main implementation risk. A small local order delays but does not solve the plant problem. The bank preferring layoffs argues against the pay cut. Low junior productivity argues for layoffs, and union refusal undermines the pay cut.
options: A survey of employees shows that 70 percent prefer a temporary pay cut to any job losses
The oldest plant has just won a small local order that covers its costs for three months
The bank has said it prefers layoffs to pay cuts
Junior workers have the lowest productivity in the firm
The union has refused to discuss a pay cut at all
items.passage: A textile firm with 1,200 employees must cut annual costs by 12 crore rupees after losing its largest export order. The management team has three options. First, close the oldest plant, which employs 180 workers, and move 60 of them to other plants with retraining. Second, lay off 120 junior workers across all plants, keeping every plant open. Third, cut pay by 8 percent for all employees for one year, with a promise to restore pay if orders return. The union opposes all three options and has warned of a strike if any worker is dismissed. The oldest plant has the highest accident rate and the oldest machines, but it is the only employer in its small town, and closing it would devastate the local economy. The junior workers are mostly under 30 and were hired in the last two years, while the senior staff have families and housing loans. The pay cut would hit senior staff hardest in absolute rupees, but it would keep every job. The board wants a decision within a month, before the next export season, and the bank that funds the firm has asked for a credible cost-cutting plan before it renews the working capital loan. The bank has asked for a written plan within a month and has said the working capital loan will be reviewed at the same time. The oldest plant's machines are 25 years old and its maintenance costs have doubled in three years, while the other two plants have newer machines and spare capacity. The union has 900 members across the three plants and has already held a meeting to discuss a strike vote. The export season starts in two months and the firm needs its full workforce to meet the orders it has already accepted.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support choosing the pay cut over the other two options?
items.set_title: DM6: The Plant That Must Shrink

items.explanation: Sharing the finances, consulting genuinely and publishing criteria gives the decision legitimacy and reduces strike risk, even when the outcome hurts some employees. Announcing the cheapest option or deciding in private destroys trust. Letting each plant decide fragments a firm-wide problem. The bank is a lender, not the decision maker on employment.
options: Announce the cheapest option immediately so the bank is reassured
Share the full financial position with the union, consult genuinely on the three options, and publish the criteria for the final choice with support for those affected
Let each plant manager choose separately for their own plant
Ask the bank to choose the option it prefers
Decide in private and present the decision as final with no discussion
items.question: What process should the management follow before choosing an option?
items.set_title: DM6: The Plant That Must Shrink

items.explanation: If the oldest plant is the only site that can house next year's essential machines, closing it destroys future capacity and makes the cut short-sighted. The high accident rate supports closing. Cheap retraining supports closing. The town impact and the possible return of the order are relevant but do not show the closure harms the firm's own future operations as directly as losing the only suitable site.
options: The oldest plant has the highest accident rate of the three plants
Retraining the 60 transferred workers would cost less than expected
The oldest plant is the only one with space to install the new machines the firm needs next year
The town has no other large employer
The export order that was lost may return in two years
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the case for closing the oldest plant?
items.set_title: DM6: The Plant That Must Shrink

items.explanation: A history of regulatory fines for unpublished prioritisation makes first-come-first-served the safest rule, since any other order risks a penalty and a public finding of unfairness. Rebooked passengers already being compensated weakens their claim but is not the strongest support. A bank loan helps cash flow but does not choose the order. Voucher popularity and rival cancellations do not justify the queue order.
options: Passengers who rebooked have already received free meals and hotel stays
The bank has offered a short-term loan to cover refunds
Vouchers with a bonus are popular with leisure travellers
The regulator has previously fined airlines that prioritised some passengers over others without a published rule
Rival airlines have also cancelled flights this month
items.passage: A low-cost airline cancelled 400 flights over two weeks after a software failure in its crew rostering system. Around 60,000 passengers are owed refunds totalling 90 crore rupees, and the refund queue is growing because the call centre can process only 2,000 cases a day. Passengers are posting screenshots of failed refund attempts on social media, and the aviation regulator has asked for a daily report. The airline's cash position is tight after the cancellations, and paying all refunds at once would breach a loan covenant with its bank. The operations head wants to prioritise refunds for passengers who rebooked on the airline, arguing that they are the most valuable customers. The customer service head wants to process refunds strictly in the order received, arguing that fairness is the only defensible rule. The finance head wants to offer travel vouchers instead of cash refunds, with a 10 percent bonus, arguing that most passengers will accept and that cash will be preserved. The law requires cash refunds for cancellations initiated by the airline, but the voucher offer could be presented as a choice rather than a replacement. The chief executive must announce a plan today, before the evening news cycle, and the announcement will be read by passengers, the regulator, the bank and rival airlines. The regulator has asked for a daily report on refunds processed and on complaints received, and has warned that it may publish the figures. Passengers are sharing screenshots of failed refund attempts on social media, and a consumer group has collected 5,000 complaints in a week. The bank has said the loan covenant allows a short delay if the airline presents a credible repayment plan. The airline's call centre staff are working overtime, but the backlog is still growing by 1,000 cases a day.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support processing refunds strictly in the order received?

items.explanation: Cash refunds in order received, with a published timetable and daily regulator reporting, meets the legal duty and is fair and verifiable, while vouchers as an option preserve cash from those who choose them. Vouchers-only breaches the cash-refund duty. Social-media-only refunds are arbitrary. A 24-hour promise cannot be kept. Silence until the bank agrees leaves passengers and the regulator without a plan.
options: Vouchers for all passengers with no cash option mentioned
Refunds only for passengers who complain on social media
A promise to pay everyone within 24 hours even though the call centre cannot process that fast
No announcement until the bank agrees to new loan terms
Cash refunds for all, processed in the order received, with a published timetable, daily progress reports to the regulator, and vouchers offered only as an optional choice
items.question: What should the chief executive announce today?

items.explanation: Preserving cash is a benefit to the airline, not a criticism of the voucher-only offer, so it is the exception. Breaching the legal duty, forcing unusable value on passengers, unequal treatment of the unaware, and damaging trust are all genuine criticisms of hiding the cash option.
options: It breaches the legal duty to offer cash refunds for airline-initiated cancellations
It forces passengers who may never fly again to accept value they cannot use
It preserves the airline's cash during a difficult period
It treats passengers unequally if some are unaware they have a cash right
It damages trust when passengers discover the cash option was hidden
items.question: All of the following are valid criticisms of offering vouchers as the only refund option EXCEPT
A trader buys an article for Rs 900. He marks it 40% above the cost price and then allows a discount of 10% on the marked price. What is his profit percentage?
items.explanation: The marked price is Rs 900 x 1.4 = Rs 1260. After a 10% discount the selling price is Rs 1260 x 0.9 = Rs 1134, so the profit is Rs 234 on Rs 900, which is 26%. Adding 40% and subtracting 10% to get 30% is wrong because the discount applies to the marked price, not the cost price.

items.question: A train 300 metres long crosses a signal pole in 15 seconds. What is the speed of the train in km/h?
options: 60 km/h
80 km/h
72 km/h
54 km/h
90 km/h
items.explanation: The speed is 300/15 = 20 metres per second. Converting with the factor 18/5 gives 20 x 18/5 = 72 km/h. Forgetting the conversion, or multiplying by 5/18 instead of 18/5, gives the wrong options.

items.question: The average of 6 numbers is 42. If one number is removed, the average of the remaining numbers becomes 40. What is the number that was removed?
items.explanation: The sum of the 6 numbers is 6 x 42 = 252. The sum of the remaining 5 is 5 x 40 = 200. The removed number is the difference, 252 - 200 = 52. The other options come from miscomputing one of the two sums.

items.question: Five distinct positive integers have an average of 20. What is the maximum possible value of the largest integer?
items.explanation: The sum of all 5 values is 5 x 20 = 100. To make the largest value as big as possible, the other 4 values must be as small as possible while staying distinct and positive, so they are 1, 2, 3, 4, summing to 10. The largest value is therefore 100 - 10 = 90. Forgetting that the values must be distinct, or using the average itself as the maximum, gives the wrong options.

items.question: A can finish a piece of work in 15 days and B can finish the same work in 20 days. Working together, in how many days will they finish the work?
options: 7 days
60/7 days
10 days
8 days
9 days
items.explanation: A does 1/15 of the work per day and B does 1/20, so together they do 1/15 + 1/20 = 7/60 of the work per day. The time needed is the reciprocal, 60/7 days. Averaging the two times is wrong because rates add, not times.

items.question: Two concentric circles have radii 7 cm and 14 cm. What is the area of the ring between them? (Use pi = 22/7)
options: 308 sq cm
462 sq cm
616 sq cm
392 sq cm
500 sq cm
items.explanation: The ring area is pi x (14 squared - 7 squared) = (22/7) x (196 - 49) = (22/7) x 147 = 462 sq cm. Using only the outer circle, or subtracting the radii before squaring, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the maximum area of a rectangle that can be inscribed in a circle of radius 10 cm?
options: 200 sq cm
314 sq cm
100 sq cm
400 sq cm
150 sq cm
items.explanation: The largest inscribed rectangle is a square whose diagonal is the diameter, 20 cm, so its side is 20/sqrt(2) = 14.14 cm and its area is (14.14) squared = 200 sq cm. In general the maximum area is 2R squared = 2 x 100 = 200 sq cm. Any non-square rectangle has a smaller area.

items.question: A right-angled triangle has legs of length 5 cm and 12 cm. What is its area?
options: 60 sq cm
39 sq cm
25 sq cm
42 sq cm
30 sq cm
items.explanation: The area of a right triangle is half the product of its legs, (1/2) x 5 x 12 = 30 sq cm. The hypotenuse is 13 cm, but it is not used for the area, and using it as a leg gives the wrong options.

items.question: A triangle has sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. What is the radius of its incircle?
options: 6 cm
5 cm
8 cm
3 cm
4 cm
items.explanation: The semi-perimeter is 21 cm and the area, by Heron's formula, is 84 sq cm. The inradius is area divided by semi-perimeter, 84/21 = 4 cm. The circumradius is a different quantity, and half of any side is not the inradius.

items.question: What is the volume of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 12 cm? (Use pi = 22/7)
options: 1540 cubic cm
1848 cubic cm
1680 cubic cm
2016 cubic cm
1320 cubic cm
items.explanation: The volume is pi x r squared x h = (22/7) x 49 x 12 = 1848 cubic cm. Forgetting to square the radius, or using the diameter, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the LCM of 12, 15 and 20?
items.explanation: The LCM of 12, 15 and 20 is found from 12 = 2 squared x 3, 15 = 3 x 5 and 20 = 2 squared x 5, so the LCM is 2 squared x 3 x 5 = 60. Any common multiple smaller than this fails to be divisible by at least one of the three numbers.

items.question: How many positive divisors does 360 have?
items.explanation: Factorising, 360 = 2 cubed x 3 squared x 5. A divisor is fixed by choosing the exponent of 2 in 4 ways, of 3 in 3 ways and of 5 in 2 ways, so the number of divisors is 4 x 3 x 2 = 24. Counting only the prime factors, or adding the exponents, gives the wrong options.

items.question: How many integers from 1 to 500 are divisible by 3 or by 7, but not by both?
items.explanation: There are 166 multiples of 3 and 71 multiples of 7 up to 500, with 23 multiples of 21 counted in both. Those counted in exactly one of the two sets number 166 + 71 - 2 x 23 = 191. The union count, 214, includes the overlap once and is a distractor.

items.question: What is the largest three-digit number divisible by both 7 and 11?
items.explanation: A number divisible by both 7 and 11 is a multiple of their LCM, 77. The largest multiple of 77 below 1000 is 12 x 77 = 924. The next multiple, 1001, has four digits, and 999 itself is not divisible by 7.

items.question: If the roots of the equation x squared - 9x + 20 = 0 are alpha and beta, what is alpha squared + beta squared?
items.explanation: The roots are 4 and 5, so alpha squared + beta squared = 16 + 25 = 41. Equivalently, (alpha + beta) squared - 2 alpha beta = 9 squared - 2 x 20 = 41. Adding the roots, or squaring their sum without the correction, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the minimum value of x squared - 6x + 13, where x is a real number?
items.explanation: Completing the square gives x squared - 6x + 13 = (x - 3) squared + 4. The squared term is never negative, so the minimum is 4, attained at x = 3. The constant term alone, or the value at x = 0, gives the wrong options.

items.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers shown is 9?
items.explanation: There are 36 equally likely outcomes. The pairs summing to 9 are (3,6), (4,5), (5,4) and (6,3), that is 4 outcomes, so the probability is 4/36 = 1/9. Counting only the unordered pairs, or including pairs that sum to 8 or 10, gives the wrong options.

items.question: In a survey of 100 people, 60 like tea, 50 like coffee and 40 like juice. 25 like both tea and coffee, 20 like both coffee and juice, 15 like both tea and juice, and 10 like all three. How many people like only tea?
items.explanation: People who like only tea are those in the tea set minus those shared with coffee or juice, adding back those counted twice in all three: 60 - 25 - 15 + 10 = 30. Forgetting to add back the triple intersection, or subtracting it, gives the wrong options.

items.question: Is the positive integer x divisible by 6? Statement I: x is divisible by 2. Statement II: x is divisible by 3.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Either statement alone is sufficient.
Neither statement alone nor both together are sufficient.
items.explanation: Divisibility by 6 needs both a factor 2 and a factor 3. Statement I alone leaves open numbers like 9 that are divisible by 3 but not 2, and statement II alone leaves open numbers like 4 that are divisible by 2 but not 3. Together they settle it, so both statements together are sufficient and neither alone is.

items.question: What is the total annual sales of product B?

diagram.caption: Quarterly sales (Rs lakh) of four products, FY 2025-26

options: Rs 840 lakh
Rs 780 lakh
Rs 880 lakh
Rs 820 lakh
Rs 920 lakh
items.explanation: Product B sold 200 + 180 + 220 + 240 = 840 lakh across the four quarters. Adding only three quarters, or using another product's row, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the percentage growth in the sales of product A from Q3 to Q4?
items.explanation: Product A rose from 180 lakh in Q3 to 210 lakh in Q4, an increase of 30 lakh on 180 lakh, which is 16.67%. Growth on the Q4 base, or on the annual total, gives the wrong options.

items.question: Which product has the highest total annual sales?
options: Product B
Product A
Product C
Product D
All equal
items.explanation: The annual totals are A: 660, B: 840, C: 480 and D: 660 lakh, so B is the highest. Product A leads in Q4 alone, but over the whole year B is ahead.

items.question: What is the total number of paid visitors in the second quarter (Apr-Jun)?

diagram.caption: Monthly website visitors (thousands) by channel, Jan-Jun 2026

options: 90 thousand
105 thousand
125 thousand
100 thousand
115 thousand
items.explanation: Paid visitors were 35 + 30 + 40 = 105 thousand in Apr, May and Jun. Adding the organic figures, or only two of the three months, gives the wrong options.

items.question: In which month was the total number of visitors (organic plus paid) the highest?
options: Jan
Feb
Jun
Mar
Apr
items.explanation: The monthly totals are 60, 70, 80, 90, 90, 110 thousand, so the highest is 110 thousand in Jun. May has the second-highest total, and the organic-only peak is also in Jun, but the question asks for the combined total.

items.question: What is the ratio of organic to paid visitors in June?
items.explanation: In June there were 70 thousand organic and 40 thousand paid visitors, a ratio of 70:40, which simplifies to 7:4. The ratio over the whole half year is different, and inverting the ratio gives the wrong options.

items.question: How many defect-free units does the factory produce per day in total?

diagram.caption: Daily production and defect rates of three machines
diagram.content: A factory has three machines. Machine M1 produces 1200 units per day with a defect rate of 5%. Machine M2 produces 900 units per day with a defect rate of 8%. Machine M3 produces 1500 units per day with a defect rate of 4%.

options: 3308 units
3528 units
3348 units
3408 units
3468 units
items.explanation: Defect-free units are M1: 1200 x 0.95 = 1140, M2: 900 x 0.92 = 828 and M3: 1500 x 0.96 = 1440, totalling 3408 per day. Adding the defect counts instead of the good units, or using the gross output, gives the wrong options.

items.question: Which machine produces the largest number of defective units per day?
options: Machine M1
Machine M3
Machine M2
M1 and M3 produce equal numbers
All three produce equal numbers
items.explanation: Defective units per day are M1: 60, M2: 72 and M3: 60, so M2 produces the most defective units. M2 has the highest defect rate, but M3's larger output gives it the same count as M1, and the rate alone does not decide the count.

items.question: Which machine has the highest proportion of defect-free output?
options: Machine M1
Machine M2
M1 and M2 together
All three are equal
Machine M3
items.explanation: The defect-free proportions are M1: 95%, M2: 92% and M3: 96%, so M3 is the highest. The machine with the largest output is not necessarily the most reliable, and the defect rate order is the reverse of this order.

items.question: Who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025?
options: Maria Corina Machado
Elon Musk
Volodymyr Zelenskyy
Greta Thunberg
Malala Yousafzai
items.explanation: Maria Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader, won the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize for her democratic struggle in Venezuela. Elon Musk and Volodymyr Zelenskyy have never won the prize, Greta Thunberg has only been nominated, and Malala Yousafzai won it in 2014, not 2025.

items.question: Which novel won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2025?
options: The Women by Kristin Hannah
James by Percival Everett
The Covenant of Water by Abraham Verghese
Demon Copperhead by Barbara Kingsolver
Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow by Gabrielle Zevin
items.explanation: James by Percival Everett won the 2025 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. It retells Adventures of Huckleberry Finn from the perspective of the enslaved man Jim. Demon Copperhead won the prize in 2023, while the other three novels were never Pulitzer winners in fiction.

items.question: The Chenab rail bridge, inaugurated in June 2025, is described as the world's highest railway arch bridge. In which Union Territory is it located?
options: Ladakh
Himachal Pradesh
Jammu and Kashmir
Uttarakhand
Sikkim
items.explanation: The Chenab rail bridge spans the Chenab river in Reasi district of Jammu and Kashmir, standing 359 metres above the riverbed. It is part of the Udhampur-Srinagar-Baramulla rail link. Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Sikkim do not host this bridge.

items.question: Who won the ICC Champions Trophy in 2025?
options: Australia
Pakistan
England
India
South Africa
items.explanation: India won the 2025 ICC Champions Trophy, beating New Zealand in the final in Dubai in March 2025. Pakistan hosted the tournament but was eliminated early, while Australia, England and South Africa were knocked out before the final.

items.question: Who was elected Pope in May 2025 following the death of Pope Francis?
options: Pope Benedict XVI
Cardinal Pietro Parolin
Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle
Cardinal Matteo Zuppi
Pope Leo XIV
items.explanation: Cardinal Robert Prevost of the United States was elected in May 2025 and took the name Pope Leo XIV, becoming the first American pope. Benedict XVI died in 2022, while Parolin, Tagle and Zuppi were prominent contenders in the conclave but were not elected.

items.question: India signed a Free Trade Agreement with which country in July 2025?
options: United Kingdom
United States
Australia
Canada
Japan
items.explanation: India signed a Free Trade Agreement with the United Kingdom on 24 July 2025 after years of negotiation, cutting tariffs on goods such as whisky, cars and textiles. India signed its trade deal with Australia in 2022, and no FTA was signed with the United States, Canada or Japan in July 2025.

items.question: Under the GST rate rationalisation that took effect in September 2025, how many main GST slabs remained?
options: Four
Two
Three
One
Five
items.explanation: The GST 2.0 rationalisation that took effect on 22 September 2025 collapsed the structure to two main slabs of 5 percent and 18 percent, with a separate 40 percent demerit rate for a few sin and luxury goods. The earlier structure had four main slabs of 5, 12, 18 and 28 percent, so one, three and five are incorrect.

items.question: Which Indian astronaut travelled to the International Space Station aboard Axiom Mission 4 in June 2025?
options: Rakesh Sharma
Kalpana Chawla
Shubhanshu Shukla
Ravish Malhotra
Sunita Williams
items.explanation: Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla travelled to the International Space Station on Axiom Mission 4 in June 2025, becoming the first Indian to reach the station. Rakesh Sharma flew to space in 1984, Kalpana Chawla flew on NASA shuttle missions, Ravish Malhotra was the 1984 backup, and Sunita Williams is an American astronaut.

items.question: Who won the men's Ballon d'Or in 2025?
options: Lamine Yamal
Kylian Mbappe
Mohamed Salah
Ousmane Dembele
Erling Haaland
items.explanation: Ousmane Dembele of Paris Saint-Germain won the 2025 men's Ballon d'Or after a season in which PSG won the UEFA Champions League. Lamine Yamal won the Kopa Trophy for the best young player, while Mbappe, Salah and Haaland were shortlisted but did not win the main award.

items.question: After the Delhi Assembly election held in February 2025, who became the Chief Minister of Delhi?
options: Arvind Kejriwal
Atishi
Manish Sisodia
Saurabh Bharadwaj
Rekha Gupta
items.explanation: Rekha Gupta of the Bharatiya Janata Party became Chief Minister of Delhi after the party won the February 2025 Assembly election. Arvind Kejriwal lost his own seat in the election, Atishi was the outgoing Chief Minister, and Sisodia and Bharadwaj did not take the post.

items.question: The 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded for the development of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). Which trio shared the prize?
options: Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi
John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino
Carolyn Bertozzi, Morten Meldal and Barry Sharpless
Emmanuelle Charpentier, Jennifer Doudna and Feng Zhang
Frances Arnold, George Smith and Gregory Winter
items.explanation: Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing metal-organic frameworks, porous materials built from metal ions and organic molecules. The Goodenough trio won in 2019 for lithium-ion batteries, the Bertozzi trio in 2022 for click chemistry, Charpentier and Doudna in 2020 for CRISPR, and the Arnold trio in 2018 for directed evolution.

items.question: The Waqf (Amendment) Act, passed by Parliament in April 2025, primarily concerns the administration of which of the following?
options: Temple trusts
Muslim charitable endowments
Sikh gurdwaras
Christian missionary schools
Jain monasteries
items.explanation: The Waqf (Amendment) Act 2025 amends the Waqf Act of 1995 and concerns waqf properties, which are charitable endowments made under Islamic law. Temple trusts, gurdwaras, missionary schools and Jain monasteries are governed by separate laws and are not covered by this Act.

items.question: Which cell organelle is known as the powerhouse of the cell?
options: Ribosome
Nucleus
Mitochondrion
Golgi body
Lysosome
items.explanation: The mitochondrion is known as the powerhouse of the cell because it generates ATP, the cell's main energy currency, through respiration. The nucleus holds genetic material, ribosomes make proteins, the Golgi body packages proteins, and lysosomes digest waste.

items.question: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place in which year?
items.explanation: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar, when troops under General Dyer fired on a peaceful gathering. The Champaran Satyagraha was in 1917, the Non-Cooperation Movement began in 1920, and 1918 and 1921 saw no such massacre.

items.question: Bharatanatyam, one of India's oldest classical dance forms, originates from which state?
options: Kerala
Andhra Pradesh
Karnataka
Odisha
Tamil Nadu
items.explanation: Bharatanatyam originates from Tamil Nadu, where it developed as a temple dance performed by devadasis. Kerala is home to Kathakali and Mohiniyattam, Andhra Pradesh to Kuchipudi, and Odisha to Odissi, while Karnataka is not the origin state of Bharatanatyam.

items.question: Match the books with their authors: 1. Godan 2. Gitanjali 3. Malgudi Days 4. Train to Pakistan. Authors: A. Rabindranath Tagore B. R.K. Narayan C. Premchand D. Khushwant Singh.
items.explanation: The correct pairing is Godan with Premchand, Gitanjali with Rabindranath Tagore, Malgudi Days with R.K. Narayan, and Train to Pakistan with Khushwant Singh. Every other option swaps at least one author, such as assigning Gitanjali to Premchand or Malgudi Days to Tagore.

items.question: Arrange the following events in chronological order: A. Battle of Buxar B. Battle of Plassey C. Third Battle of Panipat D. First War of Independence.
options: B, A, C, D
B, C, A, D
A, B, C, D
C, B, A, D
B, C, D, A
items.explanation: The correct order is Battle of Plassey in 1757, Third Battle of Panipat in 1761, Battle of Buxar in 1764, and the First War of Independence in 1857. The Battle of Plassey came first, Panipat followed four years later, Buxar came after Panipat, and 1857 was nearly a century later.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT a Fundamental Right guaranteed by the Indian Constitution?
options: Right to Equality
Right to Freedom of Religion
Right to Property
Right to Constitutional Remedies
Right against Exploitation
items.explanation: The Right to Property is not a Fundamental Right. It was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment in 1978 and is now only a legal right under Article 300A. The Right to Equality, Freedom of Religion, Constitutional Remedies and the Right against Exploitation are all Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 25 to 28, 32 and 23 to 24.

items.question: What is common to the Jnanpith Award, the Sahitya Akademi Award and the Saraswati Samman?
options: All are given directly by the Government of India
All carry a cash prize of Rs 1 crore
All were instituted before independence
All are literary awards of India
All are given only for Hindi literature
items.explanation: All three are Indian literary honours. The Jnanpith is given by the Bharatiya Jnanpith trust, the Sahitya Akademi Award by the Sahitya Akademi, and the Saraswati Samman by the K.K. Birla Foundation, so they are not all given directly by the government. All were instituted after independence, their cash prizes differ, and all cover multiple Indian languages, not only Hindi.

items.question: The headquarters of the World Bank is located in which city?
options: New York
Geneva
London
Paris
Washington, D.C.
items.explanation: The World Bank is headquartered in Washington, D.C. in the United States. The United Nations is headquartered in New York, the World Trade Organization in Geneva, and neither London nor Paris hosts the World Bank.
